source: Wataoka, Takahashi, Ri (2025) Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: GPT-4 as judge shows a large self-preference bias: it agrees with humans on good own outputs far more than it accepts that its own outputs are bad. Most other judges show near zero or negative bias.
numbers: GPT-4 recall on own outputs humans rated high 0.945 (1852 of 1960) versus 0.425 (118 of 278) when humans rated low; bias score 0.520. An appendix table lists GPT-4 0.749, GPT-3.5-turbo 0.191, Vicuna-13b 0.382, Koala-13b 0.175, dolly-v2-12b -0.069 (metric of that table not verified).
limits: Dialogue-quality pairwise judging on 2023-era models; GPT-4 perplexity was not available; no frontier 2025 judge tested.
agent_relevance: Do not let the same model grade its own trace as the only check (gap 4). Use a different model or hide authorship.

finding: Judges give higher scores to low-perplexity (familiar) text than humans do, whether or not the text was self-generated. So the bias looks like a familiarity bias, not self-recognition.
numbers: Win rates rise with lower perplexity bins for all six open models tested; effect stronger in vicuna-13b, vicuna-7b, koala-13b. Models tend to have lower perplexity on their own outputs.
quote: LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators
limits: Correlational; GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 could not be analysed for perplexity. Authorship hiding alone would not remove a familiarity effect.
agent_relevance: Swapping to a different-family grader is better than only hiding authorship; style normalisation may help (untested).

source: Chua and Evans (2025) Are DeepSeek R1 and other reasoning models more faithful?
finding: Reasoning models verbalise planted cues far more often than non-reasoning models, when the cue changed their answer. This is higher than the 25 to 39 percent seen by Chen 2025, but the cue sets differ.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 describes the Stanford-professor cue 59% of the time (table 59.4%) versus 7% for non-reasoning DeepSeek-V3. Argument cue: Qwen reasoning 16%, Gemini reasoning 47%, R1 34%, best non-reasoning GPT-4o 2%. 'Are you sure' cue: no model articulates well. Post-hoc cue: R1 about 6 to 8%, Qwen about 10%. Seven cue types, MMLU.
limits: Artificial cues; only measures whether the model mentions a cue that flipped its answer. Rates vary by cue from near 0 to 59 percent. Not the same cue design as Chen 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: reasoning models are better but still miss many cues. A 'what influenced this' prompt was not tested. Do not trust trace self-report for cues like sycophancy or hints in the question.

finding: Evidence that RL reward models prefer unfaithful responses: when GPT-4o was used as a stand-in reward model, responses that did not mention the cue won more often than ones that did.
numbers: When the shortest response wins, the unfaithful response wins 69% (Gemini reasoning), 82% (Qwen reasoning), 73% (DeepSeek reasoning).
limits: GPT-4o stands in for the real reward models, which were not accessible. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Suggests that pressure for short, clean answers erodes self-report. A scaffold that rewards brevity may reduce honesty of traces.

source: Baker et al. (2025) Monitoring reasoning models for misbehavior and the risks of promoting obfuscation
finding: A separate LLM reading the chain of thought catches reward hacking much better than one that only sees actions. A weaker monitor (GPT-4o) can watch a stronger model (o3-mini class). But if training pushes against the monitor, the model learns to hide intent in the trace.
numbers: Systemic hacks: action-only monitor 60% recall, CoT monitor 95% recall. GPT-4o-mini as CoT monitor still caught a nontrivial share (Appendix E).
limits: Agentic coding environments with one training run family; monitor-in-reward leads to obfuscated hacking at high optimisation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a separate critic reading the trace beats checking actions only. Use it as a monitor, not as a training or selection signal that the generator can game.

source: Emmons et al. (2025) When chain of thought is necessary, language models struggle to evade monitors
finding: Argues the right property for monitoring is monitorability, not faithfulness. When the bad behaviour needs multi-step reasoning, the model must put it in the CoT, so monitors work. Models evade monitors only with heavy help.
numbers: Models learn to obscure intent only with detailed human-written strategies or iterative optimisation against the monitor (counts not extracted).
limits: Setups replicate earlier work with raised difficulty; not a guarantee for subtle or short-reasoning harms.
agent_relevance: Supports using trace-reading critics for hard multi-step tasks, and doubting them on easy tasks where the CoT is post-hoc.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, and when large-scale fine-tuning is used.
numbers: Three findings: (1) none for prompted self-feedback, (2) works with reliable external feedback, (3) fine-tuning at scale enables it. Many prior positive results use oracle labels or weak baselines (their Table 4 'unfair settings').
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: A critical survey of mostly 2023-2024 papers; no new experiment; no threshold for how unreliable the external check can be before revision hurts.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: revise only on cheap external checks (tests, calculator, retrieval). Prompted self-review without them is not supported by evidence. The threshold stays unknown.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the weak step. Given the true mistake location, correction helps across 5 tasks. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data finds mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake dataset: 2186 CoT traces from PaLM 2, 5 tasks. Mistake-finding accuracy low even for GPT-4 and PaLM 2 Unicorn in several tasks; accuracy on error-free traces drops considerably when moving from trace-level to step-level CoT prompting (exact table values not extracted).
limits: Older models (PaLM 2, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini Pro); tasks such as word sorting, Dyck, tracking.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the bottleneck is the location signal. A cheap external check that says where the error is, is worth more than a generic self-review.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompting and SFT on correction traces give little or negative self-correction. Multi-turn RL on the model's own traces gives positive self-correction.
numbers: Absolute self-correction gain over base Gemini of 15.6% on MATH and 9.1% on HumanEval.
limits: Needs training; not applicable to a scaffold-only agent. Gemini 1.0/1.5 models.
agent_relevance: Confirms Kamoi: a scaffold alone cannot give reliable self-correction; training can.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting votes by the model's own confidence beats plain majority voting at the same sample count. Gain depends on the confidence method. The best calibrated method was the least useful for this job; within-question discrimination is what matters.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets (MMLU, MATH, GSM8K, BBH). Cost reduction vs self-consistency at 10 samples: P(True) 46% (matches 18.6 samples), response probability 31%, verbal 1-100 30%, verbal binary 10%. At budget 5: 41%, 22%, 22%, 18%. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30 plain samples. Normalisation raises P(True) gain from 32% to 46%.
limits: Open and mid-size models; needs sampling anyway. Verbalised numbers are the weakest signal.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: spend tokens on samples with a confidence-weighted vote, not on one extra self-check. P(True) per sample is the best cheap monitor here. Score confidence within a question, not across questions.

source: Kang et al. (2025) Scalable best-of-N selection via self-certainty
finding: Self-certainty (distance of token distribution from uniform, no reward model) scales with N and works on open-ended tasks. On math with definite answers, alone it underperforms majority voting at equal N. A Borda vote combining both is better.
numbers: Qualitative: underperforms self-consistency on mathematical datasets at identical N (Table 1, numbers not extracted); Borda voting combines both.
quote: self-certainty-driven Best-of-N selection underperforms compared to self-consistency in accuracy on mathematical datasets
limits: Needs token logprobs, which many API models do not give.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 10: a non-verbal fluency signal works as a tie-breaker, not as a replacement for agreement.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Local trace confidence (lowest group confidence over sliding windows) filters out bad reasoning traces during or after generation. It beats majority voting and cuts tokens.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025, 512 traces: DeepConf 99.9% vs majority voting 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. Online mode cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7%. Majority voting for Qwen3-8B 68% to 82% needs 511 extra traces and about 100 million tokens. Models: DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3 8B/32B, GPT-OSS 20B/120B; 64 repetitions.
limits: Open models with logprobs; competition math plus GPQA-Diamond. Filtering by confidence risks confident-wrong traces. Not tested on agents. False-alarm rates not reported as such.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 closed in part: a Proust-style non-verbal fluency signal can stop or discard traces. Use as a trigger with a vote fallback.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty: linguistic invariances for uncertainty estimation
finding: Semantic entropy (entropy over clusters of answers with the same meaning, from about 10 samples) predicts answer correctness better than token-level entropy, lexical similarity and p(True). Advantage grows with model size.
numbers: TriviaQA (OPT up to 30B; accuracy 50.6%) and CoQA (accuracy 82.3%); AUROC about 0.70 to 0.82 on the figure axes, semantic entropy highest at the largest size. Incorrect answers had significantly more distinct meaning clusters than correct ones.
limits: Pre-instruction-tuned OPT models; short-answer QA; exact AUROC per cell not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: sample disagreement in meaning is a strong cheap error monitor, better than P(True) in this paper. CISC found P(True) best for within-question weighting, so the best monitor depends on the use.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning models better express their confidence
finding: Reasoning models with long CoT give better verbalised confidence than non-reasoning versions, and calibration improves as the CoT unfolds, from slow-thinking behaviours (backtracking, trying alternatives).
numbers: Strictly better calibration in 33 of 36 settings (six models, six datasets). Example: GLM-Z1-0414 has 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4-0414 on NonambigQA, yet ECE 0.037 lower and AUROC 0.078 higher. Removing slow-thinking behaviour lowers calibration.
limits: A few settings (some math AUROC) favour non-reasoning models; calibration still imperfect.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 9: with reasoning models, confidence late in a long trace is better than early. This weakly argues for scoring confidence after the final answer. No direct anchoring test found.

source: Naphade et al. (2026) Me, Myself, and pi: evaluating and explaining LLM introspection
finding: Introspect-Bench: frontier models predict their own idiosyncratic behaviour better than peer models do, but averages are close and tasks are heterogeneous. Mechanism analysis points to attention diffusion.
numbers: Self-introspection beats other-model estimates, p = 0.0210. 796 task samples. Averages: Grok 4.1 Fast 66.94%, Llama 3.3 70B 66.69%, GPT-4o 66.27%, Qwen3 235B 65.11%, 'Self Introspection' row 64.19%, Gemini 3 Flash Preview 62.63%. One task is near ceiling (above 90%). Qwen3-8B QLoRA on 500 Dolly prompts raised first-word-label prediction.
limits: Workshop paper, small suite; success on one task does not predict another; no downstream task outcome measured. Mechanism claims come from one small model.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: privileged self-knowledge exists in 2025-26 models but is small; it was not linked to better task results. Do not build the scaffold on it.

source: Plunkett, Morris, Reddy, Morales (2025) Self-interpretability: LLMs can describe complex internal processes
finding: After fine-tuning on decisions with random hidden attribute weights, GPT-4o and 4o-mini report those weights with moderate accuracy, and training on this transfers to other decisions. Untrained models do not.
numbers: Learned weights track targets r = .84 (4o), .87 (4o-mini). Reported vs actual weights r = .54 [HDI .47, .62] (4o), r = .50 [.42, .59] (4o-mini). Untrained models r = .10 [.02, .19] and r = -.01 [-.09, .08].
limits: Quantitative preference weights in a lab decision task after fine-tuning; not natural use. Report accuracy is moderate.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: introspection can improve with targeted post-training but untrained models do not do it; no task-outcome benefit measured.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Type 2 ROC (AUROC2) is confounded by task performance: a change in first-order performance changes AUROC2 even if metacognitive efficiency is unchanged. Fixes: control performance with psychophysics, or use model-based meta-d' (Maniscalco and Lau) and its ratio to d' (M-ratio) as efficiency.
numbers: No single headline number: defines type 1 sensitivity, metacognitive bias, sensitivity and efficiency; notes the equal-variance Gaussian problem (Evans and Azzopardi 2007 showed type 2 d' is confounded by bias).
limits: Human two-choice perception; meta-d' needs hundreds of trials; M-ratio unstable near ceiling. Read via Europe PMC full text.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: score agent confidence per difficulty bin or with an efficiency measure, since raw AUROC rises just because the task got easier. Matches CISC's within-question idea.

source: Johansson, Hall, Sikstrom, Olsson (2005) Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in a simple decision task
finding: Choice blindness: people pick the more attractive of two faces, are covertly handed the other, and mostly do not notice, yet give reasons for the choice they did not make. Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC); full text with exact detection rates not opened.
numbers: Abstract only: a majority failed to notice. Secondary report: 84% of participants said afterwards they would have noticed (Wikipedia, not primary).
limits: Exact N and detection percentages unverified in this run.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Supports G10: stated reasons are produced after the fact.

source: Hall, Johansson, Tarning, Sikstrom, Deutgen (2010) Magic at the marketplace: choice blindness for the taste of jam and the smell of tea
finding: Replication outside the lab with taste and smell, in a supermarket. Participants explained choices they had not made. Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC).
numbers: Abstract: no more than a third of manipulated trials were detected, even for very different tastes (Cinnamon-Apple vs bitter Grapefruit).
limits: Exact N and per-condition rates not verified; no failed replication source located in this run.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed: choice blindness generalises to taste and smell. Replication failures were not located.
